lessons.title: Variables and types
paragraphs: A variable gives a value a name. You can use that name to work with the value later in your program.
In this example, name stores text and age stores a whole number. Text is written inside quotation marks; numbers are written without them.
Open the code and change the name and age. The output shows the name first, then the age on a separate line.
lessons.note: Python determines the type from the value. age = "19" stores a string, not a number.
lessons.code:
age = 19
name = "Ali"
print(name)
print(age)
lessons.exercise: Change the age to 21. Notice the difference between writing a number and writing text.

quiz.question: Which value is an integer?
quiz.explanation: Without quotation marks, 19 is an integer. "19" is a string.

lessons.title: Conditions: if / else
lessons.summary: Teach your program to make choices
paragraphs: A condition is an expression that evaluates to true or false. An if statement runs one block when the condition is true and an else block otherwise.
The expression score >= 60 checks whether the score is at least 60. A score of 85 produces Passed.
Test values at the boundary too: 59, 60, and 61. One successful example is not enough to check your condition.
lessons.note: Python uses indentation to define blocks. Both if and else need a colon.
lessons.exercise: Set the score to 59. Then try 60 to check the boundary condition.

quiz.question: If score is 60, is score >= 60 true?
quiz.explanation: The >= operator includes equality, so the condition is true for 60.

lessons.title: Loops and sums
paragraphs: A loop repeats an operation. As the counter changes, each iteration works with a new value.
The variable total starts at 0. Adding 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 gives a final sum of 15.
Identify where the loop starts and stops. An incorrect stopping condition can cause extra iterations or an infinite loop.
lessons.note: range(1, 6) does not include 6; the last value is 5.
lessons.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 6):
    total += n
print(total)
lessons.exercise: Change the upper limit to 10. The sum of the numbers from 1 to 10 should be 55.

quiz.question: What is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5?
quiz.explanation: The five numbers add up to 15. The last counter value is not the sum.

lessons.title: Tables and data
paragraphs: SQL stores data in tables. Each column defines a type of data, and each row represents a record.
CREATE TABLE defines a table, INSERT INTO adds rows, and SELECT reads the data.
lessons.note: Each run starts with a fresh SQLite database. Create the tables you need in the same source file.
lessons.exercise: Add another student and inspect the result.

quiz.question: Which statement adds a row?
quiz.explanation: INSERT INTO adds a new row.

lessons.title: Sorting and filtering
paragraphs: WHERE chooses which rows to include. ORDER BY controls the order of the results.
This example selects students with a score of at least 60 and orders them by score from highest to lowest. DESC means descending; ASC means ascending.
lessons.note: Each run starts with a fresh SQLite database. Create the tables you need in the same source file.
lessons.exercise: Change the threshold to 90. Only one student should remain.

quiz.question: Which keyword specifies descending order?
quiz.explanation: DESC orders values from highest to lowest.

lessons.title: Aggregation and grouping
paragraphs: Aggregate functions calculate one value from several rows. COUNT counts rows and AVG calculates an average.
GROUP BY puts rows with the same key into groups. Use HAVING to filter the resulting groups.
lessons.note: Each run starts with a fresh SQLite database. Create the tables you need in the same source file.
lessons.exercise: Add columns for MAX(score) and MIN(score).

quiz.question: Which expression counts rows?
quiz.explanation: COUNT(*) counts all selected rows.

lessons.title: Joining tables
paragraphs: JOIN combines related data from two tables. ON specifies which column values must match.
INNER JOIN returns matching rows from both tables. LEFT JOIN also preserves unmatched rows from the left table.
lessons.note: Each run starts with a fresh SQLite database. Create the tables you need in the same source file.
lessons.output:
name  title
----  ------
Ali   CS-101
Lola  CS-102
lessons.exercise: Add a student with a nonexistent group. Compare INNER JOIN with LEFT JOIN.

quiz.question: Which join preserves unmatched rows from the left table?
quiz.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves every row from the left table.

references.title: print()
references.summary: Prints a value to the console.
references.note: Adds a new line by default. Use the end parameter to change it.

references.title: len()
references.summary: Returns the length of a string or collection.
references.note: Indexes start at 0. The last index is one less than the length.

references.title: range()
references.summary: Represents a sequence of integers.
references.note: The stop value is excluded. The step cannot be 0.

references.title: list.append()
references.summary: Adds an element to the end of a list.
references.note: Modifies the existing list; it does not return a new list.

references.title: cout
references.summary: Writes a value to standard output.
references.note: Requires <iostream>. Use std::cout or a using declaration.

references.title: cin
references.summary: Reads a formatted value from standard input.
references.note: Reads whitespace-separated values. Use getline to read a whole line.

references.title: vector.push_back()
references.summary: Adds an element to the end of a vector.
references.note: Requires <vector>. Appending has amortized O(1) time complexity.

references.title: string.size()
references.summary: Returns the size of a string.
references.note: For UTF-8 strings, the byte count is not always the number of characters.

references.title: printf()
references.summary: Prints values using a format string.
references.note: Use %d for int and %s for a null-terminated string. Requires <stdio.h>.

references.title: scanf()
references.summary: Reads values from standard input.
references.note: Check the return value. When reading strings, limit the field width to fit the buffer.

references.title: strlen()
references.summary: Returns the length of a null-terminated string.
references.note: Requires <string.h>. The terminating null byte is not counted.

references.title: sizeof
references.summary: Gives the size of an object or type in bytes.
references.note: This is an operator, not a function. sizeof(pointer) does not give the length of an array.

references.title: console.log()
references.summary: Prints a value to the console.
references.note: JavaScript runs in a Node.js environment in this compiler.

references.title: Array.map()
references.summary: Creates a new array by transforming each element.
references.note: The result is [2, 4, 6]. This example does not modify the original array.

references.title: Array.filter()
references.summary: Creates a new array containing elements that pass a test.
references.note: The result is [2, 4]. An element is kept when the callback returns a truthy value.

references.title: JSON.parse()
references.summary: Converts JSON text into a JavaScript value.
references.note: Invalid JSON throws a SyntaxError. Use try/catch when appropriate.

references.title: println()
references.summary: Prints a value followed by a new line.
references.note: print does not add a new line; println does.

references.title: Scanner.nextInt()
references.summary: Reads the next integer.
references.example:
Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
int n = scanner.nextInt();
references.note: Requires import java.util.Scanner. Invalid input may throw an exception.

references.title: String.length()
references.summary: Returns the string length in UTF-16 code units.
references.note: This is not always the number of visible Unicode characters.

references.title: ArrayList.add()
references.summary: Adds an element to a dynamic list.
references.note: Requires import java.util.ArrayList. Use Integer rather than int for the type parameter.

references.title: fmt.Println()
references.summary: Prints values followed by a new line.
references.note: Requires import "fmt". Inserts spaces between values.

references.title: fmt.Scan()
references.summary: Reads a value from standard input.
references.note: Returns the number of items read and an error. Check the error in real applications.

references.title: append()
references.summary: Appends an element and returns the updated slice.
references.note: Save the returned slice; its backing array may have been reallocated.

references.title: len()
references.summary: Returns the length of a slice, map, array, or string.
references.note: For strings, len counts bytes, not Unicode characters.

references.title: puts
references.summary: Prints a value followed by a new line.
references.note: print usually does not add a new line.

references.title: gets
references.summary: Reads one line from standard input.
references.note: May return nil at the end of input. chomp removes the trailing record separator.

references.title: Array#map
references.summary: Creates a new array from the results of a block.
references.note: The result is [2, 4, 6]. map! changes the original array instead.

references.title: Array#select
references.summary: Selects elements that satisfy a condition.
references.note: The result is [2, 4].

references.title: SELECT
references.summary: Reads columns from a table.
references.note: Do not rely on row order without ORDER BY.

references.title: WHERE
references.summary: Filters rows using a condition.
references.example: SELECT name FROM students WHERE score >= 60;
references.note: Check for NULL with IS NULL, not = NULL.

references.title: GROUP BY
references.summary: Groups rows for aggregate calculations.
references.example: SELECT group_id, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY group_id;
references.note: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters the calculated groups.

references.title: JOIN
references.summary: Combines related tables.
references.example: SELECT s.name, g.title FROM students s JOIN groups g ON s.group_id = g.id;
references.note: Multiple matches can increase the number of rows in the result.

algorithms.title: Linear search
algorithms.summary: Check elements one by one from start to finish.
steps: Start at index 0.
Compare each element with the target.
Return the index when a match is found; otherwise continue.
Return -1 if you reach the end without a match.
algorithms.note: The array does not need to be sorted. If values repeat, this implementation returns the first matching index.

algorithms.title: Binary search
algorithms.summary: Halve the search interval in a sorted array.
steps: The array must be sorted in ascending order.
Calculate the middle index from the left and right boundaries.
If the middle value is smaller, move the left boundary up; if larger, move the right boundary down.
Return the index when found, or -1 when the interval is empty.
algorithms.note: This algorithm does not guarantee a correct answer on an unsorted array. Indexes start at 0.

algorithms.title: Bubble sort
algorithms.summary: Compare neighboring elements and move larger values to the right.
steps: Compare two neighboring elements.
Swap them if the left value is larger.
After one pass, the largest remaining value reaches the end.
Stop early when a pass makes no swaps.
algorithms.note: Useful for learning. For large datasets, usually prefer the sorting tools provided by the language.

algorithms.title: Stack — LIFO
algorithms.summary: The last element added is the first one removed.
algorithms.complexity: Push/pop at the end: amortized O(1)
steps: Create an empty stack.
Push an element onto the end.
Pop the last element.
Check that the stack is not empty before removing an element.
algorithms.note: Popping from the end of a Python list works well for stacks. Calling pop() on an empty list raises IndexError.

algorithms.title: Queue — FIFO
algorithms.summary: The first element added is the first one removed.
steps: Create an empty queue.
Add an element at the end.
Remove an element from the front.
Use deque for efficient removal from the front.
algorithms.code:
from collections import deque

queue = deque(["Ali", "Lola"])
queue.append("Vali")
print(queue.popleft())
print(queue.popleft())
algorithms.note: list.pop(0) takes O(n) time; deque.popleft() is better suited to a queue.

algorithms.title: Dictionary — hash map
algorithms.summary: Look up values by key and count repeated items.
algorithms.complexity: Lookup/insertion: average O(1), worst case O(n)
steps: Use each value as a key.
Start the count at 0 if the key is missing.
Increase the count at each occurrence.
Read the result using the key.
algorithms.note: Python dictionary keys must be hashable. A list, for example, cannot be used as a key.

algorithms.title: Linked list
algorithms.summary: Each node stores a value and a reference to the next node.
algorithms.complexity: Insert at head: O(1), search: O(n)
steps: Store value and next fields in a Node class.
Keep a head reference to the first node.
Follow next to move to the next node.
Stop when you reach None.
algorithms.note: There is no direct indexed access: you must walk through the list to reach the desired node.

algorithms.title: Breadth-first search (BFS)
algorithms.summary: Visit a graph layer by layer from a starting node.
steps: Add the starting node to the queue and the visited set.
Remove the node at the front of the queue.
Mark unvisited neighbors and add them to the queue.
Continue until the queue is empty.
algorithms.note: V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges. This implementation visits only the part reachable from the starting node.
